title: Secrets in code
bridge: A capability is like the session cookie an API hands out after login. Whoever holds it may act, so you store only its hash and compare it carefully. Except: there is no login behind it. The orchestrator mints one per run, it opens one narrow scope, and it dies with the run.
intro: The VM never holds a key, but it must still prove which run it is. It does that with a random capability for the broker and a signed run token for the gateway. This lesson builds both with node:crypto, and the habits that keep secrets out of logs.

picture.caption: The broker hands out a capability once, keeps only its hash, and checks every call against it.

steps.text: opens a run scope; the broker makes randomBytes(32) and returns it once
stores only sha256(capability) next to the scope
hashes what it got and compares digests in constant time
the audit line names the run and the call, never the capability

p: A capability is a long random string that grants one scope. node:crypto's randomBytes(32) gives 32 bytes from the operating system's secure random source. As hex that is 64 characters. Byte's workflow makes the same thing with openssl rand -hex 32.
Math.random() is not for secrets. It is built for speed, and its output can be predicted.
sections.because: We use 32 random bytes because nobody can guess 256 bits, so the token needs no password behind it.

notes.text: Built into Node. The ticket list: randomBytes, createHash, createHmac, timingSafeEqual.
A hash turns any text into 32 bytes. The same input always gives the same digest.
Secure random bytes. toString("hex") makes them safe to put in a header.
The caller hands the capability to the VM once and stores only the digest.

sections.h: Store a hash, not the token
p: A hash is one-way: from the digest you cannot get the capability back. The broker stores only sha256(capability) in Postgres. If that table leaks, nobody can call the broker with what they found.
Passwords need slow hashes like bcrypt, because people pick guessable ones. A 256-bit random token cannot be guessed, so a plain sha256 is enough.
sections.because: We look a scope up by digest because then the database never holds anything a thief could replay.

notes.text: Byte has one capability per job and compares it directly. Nova's broker has many, so it looks up the digest.
The standard header form: Authorization: Bearer <token>. Anything else is 401.
The digest of what the VM sent. Only digests ever reach the database.
A query parameter: pg sends the value apart from the SQL, so it can never change the query.
A scope dies with its run. An expired one is the same as a missing one.

p: a === b on strings stops at the first character that differs. A wrong guess with a right first half takes slightly longer. Over many tries an attacker can measure that and find the token piece by piece.

timingSafeEqual always compares every byte, so the time says nothing. It takes two Buffers of the same length and throws a RangeError otherwise. Comparing two sha256 digests avoids that: both are always 32 bytes.
sections.because: We compare digests with timingSafeEqual because === leaks through timing and timingSafeEqual needs equal lengths.

notes.text: presented is what came in the header; digest is what we stored.
Hash first, so even a 3-character guess becomes 32 bytes and no RangeError is thrown.
Comparing raw strings of different lengths throws. Check lengths first, or compare digests.

p: The gateway's run token carries claims: agent, Jira key, run, expiry and a per-agent epoch. The orchestrator signs them with an HMAC, a hash mixed with a secret key. Only a holder of the key can make a valid signature.

The claims are base64url, which is an encoding, not encryption. Anyone can read them. So a claim may say which run this is, but never hold a secret. The signing key lives in Vault at infrastructure/ai-agents/gateway.

To check a token, the gateway splits it at the dot into claims and signature. It computes the HMAC of the claims again with the same key, and compares the two with timingSafeEqual. If anyone changed one claim, the signatures differ and the answer is 401. Only then does it check the expiry and the epoch.
sections.because: We sign instead of storing because the gateway can then check a token with no database call.

notes.text: The gateway's real claims also carry an epoch: bumping it kills every live token of that agent.
HMAC-SHA256 of the body with the key. Change one character of the body and the signature changes.
Token = claims, a dot, the signature.
The clock is a parameter, so a test can pass a fake time (lesson p1-6).
Length first, then timingSafeEqual. A wrong length is a wrong token anyway.
exp is in seconds like other tokens; Date.now() is in milliseconds.

p: A secret in a log is a secret for everyone who can read logs. So no token, key or capability goes into a log line, an error message, a URL or a test snapshot. The gateway logs method, path, status and latency only, and a test fails if request text reaches the logs.
Byte's broker has a secret guard. Before it returns any output, it checks that the token and the capability are not in it. Here is the idea as a lab file.
sections.because: We guard the output in code because a stray print in some later PR is the usual way a secret leaks.

notes.text: A named error, so a test can expect exactly this refusal.
Skip empty strings: every text includes the empty string.
Refuse, and never print the secret in the error message itself.

callout.text: No keys in the VM. The capability and the run token are not keys. They open one run's scope, our services check them, and they die with the run.

sections.h: The server asks for a capability
p: Now the notes service from p1-3 checks a capability, like the broker. server.ts exports createApp(digest) instead of a ready server. main.ts makes a capability, prints it once, and passes the digest in.
/health still needs no auth, so probes work. Everything else without the right capability gets 401 before any body is read.
sections.because: We pass in the digest, so the server never sees the capability and tests can give it their own.

notes.text: The token from the header, or an empty string when there is none.
A function that builds a server for one digest. Each test can make its own.
The list now lives inside createApp, so two servers never share notes.
Checked before the body is read: an unknown caller costs us almost nothing.

lab.faded: Forge a token. Split a valid token at the dot. Build a new body with agent set to admin, and glue it to the old signature. Left to you: print verifyToken of the forged token and explain in one sentence why it is null.

quiz.q: Why compare secrets with timingSafeEqual instead of ===?

options.text: === can return sooner on the first wrong character, so timing leaks how much of a guess was right
options.why: timingSafeEqual always compares every byte, so the time says nothing.

options.text: === does not work on strings that long
options.why: It works; it is the timing that leaks.
It is not about speed; it is deliberately constant.

quiz.q: The broker's run_scopes table leaks. What can an attacker do with the sha256 digests?

options.text: Send a digest as the Bearer token and act as that run
options.why: The broker hashes what it receives; a digest of a digest matches nothing.

options.text: Reverse a digest to get the capability back
options.why: sha256 is one-way, and 256 random bits cannot be guessed.

options.text: Nothing useful: they cannot turn a digest into a working capability
options.why: That is why only digests are stored.

quiz.q: Which may go inside a gateway run token's claims?

options.text: The run id and the expiry time
options.why: Claims are readable by anyone; they say who and until when, nothing secret.

options.text: The workload's Anthropic key, so the gateway need not look it up
options.why: Claims are base64url, not encrypted. The key would reach the VM.

options.text: The HMAC signing key, so the gateway can verify the token
options.why: The gateway has the key from Vault; putting it in the token lets anyone sign.

words.plain: A random per-run token that opens one scope in the broker; it is not a key and dies with the run.
node:crypto's secure random source; randomBytes(32) gives 256 bits.
A one-way 32-byte fingerprint of a text; we store it instead of the token.
Compares two equal-length Buffers in constant time; throws on different lengths.
A hash mixed with a secret key; only a key holder can make a valid signature.
The gateway's signed token with agent, Jira key, run, expiry and epoch; readable, not secret.
Code that refuses to output any text containing a known secret, like Byte's broker has.

tickets.why: The broker makes capabilities with randomBytes(32), stores only sha256 digests, and never logs a token.
The gateway's run tokens are HMAC-signed and checked with timingSafeEqual; access logs hold no content.
The claim activity mints both per run and writes them to /run/nova/ with mode 0600.

remember: Make secrets with randomBytes, store only a hash, compare with timingSafeEqual, sign with HMAC, and never log one.
